title: Disgrace or Democracy? Trump Attacks His Own Justices as SCOTUS Strikes Down His Tariffs
subtitle: In a 6-3 ruling, the Supreme Court found that Trump's sweeping IEEPA tariffs exceeded presidential authority — prompting Trump to attack his own appointees Gorsuch and Barrett as 'an embarrassment to their families' and Vice President Vance to call the decision 'lawlessness from the Court, plain and simple'

poll.question: What do you think of the Supreme Court's tariff ruling?

options.label: Disgrace
options.description: Unelected justices sabotaged the president's right to protect American workers

options.label: Democracy
options.description: The Court correctly reined in a president who was overstepping the Constitution

conservative.headline: Judicial Coup: Activist Court Hands China a Victory by Stripping Trump's Power to Fight Back
conservative.byline: As seen on Fox News, Breitbart, The Hill
paragraphs: The Supreme Court just handed Beijing its biggest victory of the year — not through trade negotiations, but by stripping the president of his most powerful tool to defend American workers and force other nations to the table.

In a shocking 6-3 ruling on February 20, six justices — including Trump's own appointees Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett — declared that the president's IEEPA tariffs were unconstitutional, siding with foreign trading partners over American manufacturers and farmers. Vice President JD Vance didn't mince words: "This is lawlessness from the Court, plain and simple."

President Trump, who had used the tariffs to bring dozens of countries to the negotiating table, was furious — and rightly so. He called Gorsuch and Barrett's votes "an embarrassment to their families." He blasted the two as "just being fools and lap dogs for the RINOs and the radical left Democrats" and called them "very unpatriotic and disloyal to our Constitution."

Conservative radio host Mark Levin said the court had "achieved nothing but chaos" with its ruling, calling it a "very messy and problematic" decision. Justice Clarence Thomas — one of the three dissenters — wrote a blistering dissent arguing that the majority had fundamentally misread the Constitution's allocation of war powers and foreign affairs authority to the executive branch.

The president wasted no time in adapting. Within hours of the ruling, Trump announced new tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 — initially at 10%, then raised the following day to the maximum 15% allowed under that statute. "I'm ashamed of certain members of the court, absolutely ashamed for not having the courage to do what's right for our country," Trump told reporters, but made clear he would use every available legal tool to maintain America's leverage.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed the administration would replace the rejected IEEPA tariffs by leveraging other existing trade laws, resulting in "virtually unchanged tariff revenue in 2026." Section 301 investigations are already underway, which could produce tariffs that are neither time-limited nor capped at 15%.

Six unelected judges don't get to unilaterally surrender America's economic leverage to China and the European Union. Trump's tariffs were working — countries were cutting deals, factories were returning, and the trade deficit was shrinking. This ruling is a gift to Beijing, and the justices who sided against American workers will own the consequences.

liberal.headline: The Rule of Law Wins: Supreme Court Stops Trump's Illegal Tax on Every American Family
liberal.byline: As seen on The Hill, CBS News, Washington Post
paragraphs: The Supreme Court just ruled that Donald Trump cannot unilaterally impose the largest tax increase on American families in a generation — and the president's response proved exactly why the courts need to keep checking his power.

In a landmark 6-3 ruling on February 20, the Court struck down Trump's sweeping IEEPA tariffs, which had cost the average American household $1,000 in 2025 and $1,300 in 2026 — all without a single vote in Congress. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called it "a crushing defeat for the wannabe King who did not have the authority to engage in the reckless Trump Tariffs."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was equally direct: "This is a win for the wallets of every American consumer." The ruling shields families from a tax that raised more than $160 billion for the federal government through February 20 — money taken directly from importers, businesses, and consumers who paid higher prices on everything from electronics to groceries.

But just hours after the ruling, Trump announced he was imposing new tariffs anyway — this time under Section 122, first at 10%, then immediately bumped to the maximum 15%. Legal experts immediately flagged that Trump may not even meet the preconditions required to use Section 122, which requires a finding of a "fundamental international payments problem" — not just a trade deficit.

The president's reaction to losing in court exposed the authoritarian streak his critics have warned about for years. He attacked the two Supreme Court justices he himself appointed — Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett — calling them "an embarrassment to their families" and "fools and lap dogs." When a president attacks judges by name for ruling against him, the independence of the judiciary itself is under threat.

The ruling leaves unresolved the massive question of refunds. The $160+ billion collected in illegal tariffs was remanded back to the U.S. Court of International Trade to determine what refunds importers and businesses are owed. That process could take years — meaning companies and consumers who paid illegally imposed tariffs may wait a long time for relief.

The Court didn't just protect Americans' wallets — it protected the Constitution. Congress, not the president, has the power to set tariffs. That's not a partisan position; it's in Article I. The real disgrace isn't justices doing their jobs. It's a president who believes the law doesn't apply to him — and punishes anyone who says otherwise.

factcheck.headline: What the Court Actually Ruled — And What Happens Next
paragraphs: The Supreme Court's 6-3 tariff ruling is being called both a constitutional landmark and an act of judicial overreach. Here's what the decision actually says, who voted how, and what it means going forward.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ The ruling came down February 20, 2026: The Supreme Court voted 6-3 to strike down Trump's tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), a 1977 law. The cases were Learning Resources Inc. v. Trump and V.O.S. Selections v. United States.

✓ Who voted how: Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion, joined by Justices Gorsuch, Barrett, Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson. Justices Thomas, Alito, and Kavanaugh dissented. Two of the six in the majority — Gorsuch and Barrett — were Trump appointees.

✓ The constitutional basis: Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution gives Congress — not the president — the power to "lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises" and to "regulate Commerce with foreign nations." Roberts applied the "major questions" doctrine, writing that "the president asserts the extraordinary power to unilaterally impose tariffs of unlimited amount, duration, and scope" and must show "clear congressional authorization" for such sweeping action.

✓ The tariffs were economically massive: According to the Tax Foundation, the IEEPA tariffs were the largest U.S. tax increase as a share of GDP in more than 30 years — raising more than $160 billion through February 20, 2026. They cost the average American household an estimated $1,000 in 2025 and $1,300 in 2026.

✓ Trump immediately imposed new tariffs: Within hours, Trump announced a 10% "global tariff" under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, then raised it to the 15% maximum the following day. Section 122 has a hard cap of 15% and a 150-day time limit, after which Congress must vote to extend them.

✓ Refunds are not resolved: The ruling was remanded to the U.S. Court of International Trade to determine what refunds — potentially $100–$160+ billion — are owed to importers and businesses that paid the illegal tariffs. That process could take months or years.
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: "The Court handed China a victory" — Not exactly. The ruling applies to all countries affected by IEEPA tariffs, not just China. Some of the largest tariffs struck down were on European Union goods, Canadian imports, and others. The ruling is about the legal basis for the tariffs, not who they targeted.

⚠️ Claim: "IEEPA clearly gave the president tariff authority" — Disputed. IEEPA was a 1977 law designed to handle narrow national security emergencies. It was never used to impose economy-wide tariffs before Trump. Legal scholars on both sides debated whether tariffs fell within its scope. Six justices — including two Trump appointees — concluded it did not authorize tariffs of this scope without explicit congressional authorization.

✓ Fair Point: The Court's ruling does create economic uncertainty in the short term. Companies that had been operating under the tariff regime now face an abrupt shift, and the Section 122 replacement tariffs come with legal uncertainty of their own. Treasury Secretary Bessent's pledge to maintain revenue levels through other authorities is untested.
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: "Trump is defying the Supreme Court" — Partly misleading. Trump did not defy the ruling — he complied with it by revoking the IEEPA tariffs. He then separately imposed new tariffs under a different legal authority (Section 122). Whether those new tariffs are legally valid is an open question, but using a different law is not the same as defying a court order.

⚠️ Claim: "All tariffs are now gone" — False. Only the IEEPA-based tariffs were struck down. Section 301 tariffs on China (holdovers from Trump's first term), Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum, and now the new Section 122 tariffs all remain in place.

✓ Fair Point: Trump's personal attacks on Gorsuch and Barrett — calling them "embarrassments to their families" and "fools and lap dogs" — do represent an unprecedented public attack on sitting Supreme Court justices by the president who appointed them. That behavior has few parallels in U.S. presidential history.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

This ruling is the first time the Supreme Court has directly constrained Trump's second-term economic agenda — and the 6-3 majority, crossing both liberal and conservative wings, makes it harder to dismiss as a partisan outcome. Legal scholar Frank Bowman of the University of Missouri told Al Jazeera: "This is the first time in the last year that the Supreme Court has stepped in and attempted to do something about Donald Trump's generalized attack on the rule of law."

Section 122's 150-day clock starts now. If Congress doesn't vote to extend those tariffs, they expire automatically — setting up a high-stakes showdown before the midterms. Meanwhile, the administration is accelerating Section 301 investigations that could produce new, legally grounded tariffs with no time limit.

The Bottom Line: The Court drew a clear constitutional line: broad economic policy tools require congressional authorization. Trump did not defy the ruling, but his instant pivot to a new tariff authority — and his attacks on the justices who ruled against him — signals that this legal battle over presidential trade power is far from over. Buckle up.
